title: Born-Preconditioned Learning for Iterative Neural PDE Solvers
claim: On a representative heterogeneous-medium instance, our learned preconditioner reaches the same residual in far fewer iterations than baseline iterative solvers.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: input medium, solution field, log-scale convergence curves
description: Three side-by-side panels show one example problem. The left panel is a jet-colormap heatmap of the speed of sound (a heterogeneous velocity map with blocky layered regions) with a white X marking the source location, plus a colorbar from about 1750 to 3750. The middle panel shows the real part of the resulting wavefield as a red-blue diverging heatmap with concentric oscillating wave fronts radiating from a point source and a symmetric colorbar. The right panel, Iteration History, is a semi-log line plot of relative residual against iteration. It has five colored, marker-coded curves: CBS in blue, NPBS(MgNO) in red, FGMRES+CBS in green, FGMRES+NPBS(MgNO) in orange, and FGMRES+SL in purple. The NPBS curves drop steeply within roughly 100 iterations, while the baselines need hundreds to over 1200 iterations. The eye goes first to the steep convergence curves on the right.
caption: Iteration comparison of different strategies on a representative instance from the OpenFWI CurveFault-B dataset.
abstract: Simulating high-frequency waves in spatially varying media remains challenging for both classical iterative methods and neural PDE solvers. We propose Neural Preconditioned Born Series (NPBS), a framework for learning iterative neural PDE solvers. Our guiding idea is to use a simple reference preconditioner to help learn a more effective neural preconditioner. Building on the Convergent Born Series (CBS), NPBS feeds a preconditioned residual to a neural network that predicts a solution update. We train the network to reduce the preconditioned residual after each update. The same reference preconditioner is used for the network input and the loss, giving a metric-matched training objective. Experiments on heterogeneous Helmholtz problems show reduced iteration counts across neural architectures and larger gains at higher wavenumbers. Within a Krylov solver, NPBS achieves the lowest wall-clock time in the evaluated solver comparison. The framework also extends naturally to three-dimensional problems. The same metric-matched formulation also improves convergence on convection-diffusion-reaction systems and Newton linear systems for nonlinear PDEs, indicating that NPBS provides a general framework for learning neural preconditioners.
